newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Wall St, French tax hikes hit Euro stocks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Wall St, French tax hikes hit Euro stocks.

text.p: A sharp fall on Wall Street depressed most leading European stock markets on Monday, while French company tax hikes aimed at fixing the state budget for European monetary union hit the Paris bourse.
German shares leapt in early trading after news of a major bank merger but the market soon succumbed to the bear trend provoked by Friday's heavy profit-taking on Wall Street.

On the foreign exchange markets, the dollar/mark rate reacted little to a French audit of state finances which estimated that the public deficit would be 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product this year.
This was well above the 3.0 percent target for joining a single European currency but in line with market expectations.
Wall Street's profit-taking binge on Friday, which dragged the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 130.31 points to 7,890.46, was the major depressant for Europe.

But Paris also suffered as investors felt that companies were bearing the brunt of French government efforts to cut the budget deficit by 0.4 percentage point in the drive to join economic and monetary union (EMU).

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said that to meet the target for the euro, the government would cut the deficit by 32 billion francs ($5.3 billion) with 22 billion in higher taxes on companies' profits and capital gains and 10 billion in spending cuts.
On the Paris bourse, the CAC-40 index was down 31.39 points (1.09 percent) at 2,845.30 by early afternoon.

London stocks took an early hit due to Wall Street before treading water as investors awaited Monday's U.S. opening. By midday the FTSE-100 index of blue chips was down 62.7 points or 1.29 percent at 4,814.5.
London dealers were also nervous about the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Tuesday when Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan will report to Congress on the state of the U.S. economy.

Greenspan sent stock markets plunging around the world last December when he warned investors against irrational exuberance. Since then the bull run has resumed with a vengeance, pushing the Dow briefly through 8,000 points last week before the profit-takers cashed in.
"There are a few people out there talking about a 20 percent fall on Wall Street but the same people have been predicting that sort of move for a while now," said one head trader in London.
Dealers played down the jitters, which follow a 20 percent rise in the FTSE this year.

"At this stage I can't get too bearish," said the head of equity sales at one brokerage. "Not much has changed on the inflation and interest rate outlook...Any setback at the moment is going to be a short, sharp shock but not much more than that."

Frankfurt told a different story in early trade. The IBIS index of electronic trade jumped around 80 points to a high of 4,211.67 on news that two of Germany's largest commercial banks, Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypobank, would merge.
But the mood did not last and by early afternoon the IBIS was down 17.55 points at 4,114.39.
The DAX index of floor trade was disrupted by computer problems but fell sharply after it finally got going, losing 83.49 points or 1.99 percent to 4,113.04.
Its fall, also prompted by Friday's dip in the dollar below 1.79 marks, was exaggerated as the DAX closed for the weekend before the Dow tumbled.
The dollar was robust on the foreign exchanges. It was at 1.7956 marks and 115.85 yen, compared with 1.7892 and 115.35 in late trading on Friday.

The news from Paris, much of which had been leaked, had little effect. "Most of the damage has been done in anticipation of it. The government will have prepared the market for the worst," said Tim Fox, international economist at Standard Chartered.
The mark eased slightly to 3.3792 francs from 3.3805 late on Friday and a high of 3.3810 early on Monday.
CURRENCIES AT 1100 GMT
The dollar was at 1.7956 marks and 115.85 yen, compared with 1.7892 and 115.35 in late trading on Friday.

Gold was at $328.30 after closing at $324.15 an ounce on Friday. Silver was up three cents at $4.33.
